passages.t: The third visit: ‘crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God’s power’
passages.happening:
Paul announces his coming. “This is the third time I am coming to you” (verse 1). He quotes the Law: “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (verse 1).

He has warned them before, on his second visit. Now, while away, he warns again “those who sinned earlier and everyone else: If I return, I will not spare anyone” (verse 2).

Why? Because, he says, “you are demanding proof that Christ is speaking through me” (verse 3). They will have it. Christ “is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you” (verse 3).

Then he states the truth beneath the whole letter. “For He was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God’s power. And though we are weak in Him, yet by God’s power we will live with Him to serve you” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Paul had visited Corinth twice already: once when he founded the church (Acts 18), and once on the painful visit (2:1). This would be the third.

Some in the church wanted proof that Christ really spoke through Paul. Their idea of proof was power and show. Paul answers with the cross. Jesus was crucified ‘in weakness’: he did not save himself or call down angels. Yet he was raised and lives ‘by God's power’. Weakness and power are not opposites in God's way of working. Paul's life follows the same shape.

‘I will not spare anyone’ sounds harsh. But Paul has said that he would rather not be severe (verse 10), and his whole hope is that they will turn before he comes. The warning is given so that it will not need to be carried out.
passages.ot:
Verse 1 quotes the Law. “A lone witness is not sufficient to establish any wrongdoing or sin against a man, regardless of what offense he may have committed. A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15). The rule protected people from being condemned on one person's word. Jesus used it for dealing with a brother who sins: “take one or two others along” (Matthew 18:16).

Readers take Paul's use of the rule in two ways. Some think his visits and warnings are the ‘witnesses’: he warned once, then again, and now a third time. Others think he means that any judgment on his visit will be done fairly, with proper evidence, not on rumour. Both fit the text.

The weakness of the cross is foretold in Isaiah's Servant: “He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3).
passages.asks: Paul says Christ was crucified in weakness and lives by God's power. Ask where you expect to see God's power: in strength and success, or also in weakness. And ask whether there is a warning you have been given more than once that you have not yet heeded.

passages.happening:
Now Paul turns the test around. “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves” (verse 5). He expects them to pass: “Can’t you see for yourselves that Jesus Christ is in you” (verse 5), unless they really have failed.

He hopes they will see that he has not failed the test either (verse 6). But he cares more about them than about how he looks. He prays “that you will do what is right, even if we appear to have failed” (verse 7).

“For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth” (verse 8). He is glad to be weak if they are strong, and he prays for their “perfection” (verse 9), that is, their being made whole.

That is why he writes now, “so that when I am present I will not need to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord gave me for building you up, not for tearing you down” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Listen to the testing words in these verses. ‘Test’ is dokimazō, a word used for testing metal to see if it is genuine. ‘Fail the test’ is adokimos, used of a coin or metal that is false. It comes three times here, in verses 5, 6 and 7. The Corinthians had been testing Paul. Now he asks them to test themselves.

But the question is not whether they are perfect. It is whether ‘Jesus Christ is in you’. Paul thinks they will find that he is. His own proof as an apostle is the church itself. If Christ is in them, then the man who brought them the gospel is not a fake.

‘Perfection’ in verse 9 is katartisis. It comes only here in the New Testament. A related verb is used for fishermen mending their nets (Mark 1:19). Paul's hope is for a church that is mended and whole.

Verse 10 repeats what Paul said in 10:8. Authority in the church exists ‘for building you up, not for tearing you down’.
passages.ot:
Israel's prophets and poets called God's people to examine themselves. “Let us examine and test our ways, and turn back to the LORD” (Lamentations 3:40). David asked God to do the searching: “Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my concerns. See if there is any offensive way in me; lead me in the way everlasting” (Psalm 139:23-24).

Testing metal is an Old Testament picture too. “A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, but the LORD is the tester of hearts” (Proverbs 17:3).

‘Building up, not tearing down’ comes from God's call to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:10).
passages.hard:
Does ‘Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith’ mean that Christians should keep doubting whether they are saved?

No. Read the verse in its setting. Some in Corinth were testing Paul, asking whether Christ really spoke through him. Paul turns the test back on them. And he expects them to pass: ‘Can't you see for yourselves that Jesus Christ is in you?’ The test is whether Christ is present, not whether a life is flawless.

Some readers have taken this verse as a command to search their hearts again and again for proof that they are truly saved, and they never find enough. That is not what Paul asks. Healthy self-examination looks first to Christ, not to one's own record. It leads to turning back to God and to confidence, not to despair.

Christians describe assurance, the confidence that one belongs to God, in different ways. Some stress that it rests above all on God's promises in Christ, with self-examination only confirming it. Some stress the evidence of a changed life. Some stress the Spirit's inner witness: “The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children” (Romans 8:16). Churches also differ on whether a true believer can finally fall away. These notes do not choose. The note on Romans 8:31-39 and the Honest Answer ‘Can you lose your salvation?’ set out the views.

If you are a person whose conscience never rests, who keeps checking whether you have really believed, hear John's words: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (1 John 3:20). The note on 7:8-12 says more about guilt that will not lift. Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul asked the Corinthians to look for Christ in themselves before judging him. Ask whether you are quicker to test others than yourself. Then ask the question Paul asks, gently and honestly: where do you see that Christ is in you? Look first to him, not to your own record.

passages.t: ‘The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit’
passages.happening:
Paul ends with short, warm commands. “Finally, brothers, rejoice! Aim for perfect harmony, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you” (verse 11).

“Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints send you greetings” (verses 12 and 13).

And then the blessing. “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
After four hard chapters, the letter ends in peace. ‘Aim for perfect harmony’ uses the same root as ‘perfection’ in verse 9: be mended, be made whole.

A kiss was a normal greeting among family and close friends in that world. Paul asks believers to greet each other this way as one family, and he calls it ‘holy’, set apart for God. He asks the same in other letters (Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20). About a hundred years later, the Christian writer Justin, in Rome, described believers greeting one another with a kiss when the prayers of their gathering were finished. Many churches today share a greeting of peace in worship.

Some Bibles join verses 12 and 13, so that the blessing is numbered 13:13 there. The words are the same.

‘The fellowship of the Holy Spirit’ uses koinōnia, the word Paul used for sharing in the collection (8:4). It can mean the fellowship the Spirit creates among believers, or our sharing in the Spirit himself. Both are true to Paul.
passages.ot:
Israel's priests spoke a blessing over the people in God's name. “May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24-26). Paul's blessing has the same purpose, and it ends a letter as that blessing ended Israel's worship.

The God of love and peace is the God Israel knew. “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6).

And the unity Paul asks for is sung in the psalms: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!” (Psalm 133:1).
passages.hard:
What does the closing blessing say about God?

Paul names three together: the Lord Jesus Christ, God, and the Holy Spirit. Each gives something: grace, love, fellowship. He does not explain how they are related. He simply blesses the church in all three names at once, as if that were the most natural thing in the world. Jesus told his followers to baptize “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

This verse is an early witness to the faith the church came to state in its creeds: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Nicene Creed confesses the Son as ‘very God of very God’ and the Holy Spirit as ‘the Lord and Giver of Life’. That is the faith Christians everywhere hold, not one opinion among several. Paul wrote this about twenty-five years after the cross, long before the creeds. The creeds did not invent it. They put into words what the church had been praying all along.

How can God be one and three? The site's Honest Answer, ‘How can God be three and one?’, sets out the strongest objections and what the creeds claim. The Bible Explorer's film ‘Who God is’ tells it simply.
passages.asks:
Paul ends a hard letter with grace, love and fellowship. Ask which of the three you most need today: the grace of Christ, the love of God, or the fellowship of the Spirit. Then think of one person you could greet in peace this week, especially someone you have been at odds with.

2 Corinthians ends here. Galatians comes next in the Bible, Paul's sharp letter about freedom in Christ.
